summary: Gives examples of SDP offer/answer exchanges, including codec negotiation, hold and resume, and adding or removing media streams. It shows multiple media types, one-way and inactive streams, and dynamic payload types, and also common third-party call control examples. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Worked examples of two phones negotiating how a call will work, like sample conversations in a language book.

questions: how to put a call on hold with sdp
what does port 0 mean in sdp
subtitle: Worked examples of two parties using SDP offers and answers to agree on codecs, hold calls and add or drop streams.

tldr.problem: The SDP offer/answer model can be hard to apply correctly, and implementers need concrete cases showing what each side should send.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through exchanges between two parties, Alice and Bob, with full offers and answers: codec negotiation, hold and resume, adding and deleting media streams and third party call control flows.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational set of examples that defines no new protocol. It builds on the offer/answer model of RFC 3264 and the SDP of RFC 2327.

today: RFC 4317 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted or updated. It only illustrates the offer/answer model of RFC 3264 and defines no protocol of its own.

sections.title: What the Examples Cover
sections.content:
The document gives offer/answer examples of the Session Description Protocol (SDP), based on the offer/answer model of RFC 3264. The SDP itself is as defined in RFC 2327. The offers and answers are assumed to be carried by a protocol such as the Session Initiation Protocol (RFC 3261).

In every example two parties, Alice and Bob, exchange an offer and an answer, and in some cases a second offer and answer. The examples show several media types, bidirectional, unidirectional and inactive streams, and dynamic payload types. The RFC notes that the subject line (s=) in each example contains a single space character.
sections.eli5: Alice and Bob are two callers who trade little notes saying what they can do. The RFC shows many sample note swaps.

sections.title: Codec Negotiation and Selection
sections.content:
In the first example Alice offers audio codecs PCMU, PCMA and iLBC (payload types 0, 8 and 97) and video codecs H261 and MPV. Bob answers with one of each, so the session uses only PCMU audio and MPV video. Payload type 97 is a dynamic payload type for iLBC.

Other examples show how the answer shapes the call. If Alice can support only one audio codec at a time, she makes a second offer with just that one codec. The version number in the o= line is incremented in both messages of that second exchange. A declined stream stays in the SDP with its port set to zero. A dynamic payload type may change between offer and answer (97 to 99 in one example) because the same codec is referenced.

Further cases: separate audio streams for normal audio and for telephone-events (RFC 2833 tones, for DTMF); a stream with a different connection address for video than for audio, common in conferencing where mixing uses different servers; and adding a second video codec so that the parties can switch without another exchange. When Bob changes his media address and Alice accepts with the same SDP as before, she does not increment the version number.
sections.eli5: Alice lists all the ways she can talk. Bob picks the ones he also knows. If she wants to be sure of one way, she asks again with only that one.

sections.title: Hold and Resume
sections.content:
Hold is expressed with the direction attributes sendonly and recvonly. In one example Alice calls Bob, but when Bob answers he places Alice on hold: his answer marks the audio stream a=sendonly and uses a placeholder connection address. In his second offer, Bob takes Alice off hold. Alice changes her port number in her second answer, and the media session is then active. The RFC notes a=sendrecv could be present in the second exchange, and that this is a common flow in third party call control.

A second example has two audio streams, a bidirectional audio stream and a send-only telephone event stream. Bob puts only the audio stream on hold, not the tone stream, and Alice answers with SDP identical to her initial offer.
sections.eli5: To pause a call, one side says it will only send, not listen. To resume, it sends a fresh note with the normal settings.

sections.title: Adding and Deleting Streams
sections.content:
A second exchange can add a stream. In one example the first exchange sets up a single audio stream and the second adds an audio stream for telephone events, supplied by Bob's media server (a different connection address) to receive RFC 2833 telephone-events, typically DTMF digits, from Alice. In another, an audio-only session using PCMU gets a video stream added by Alice and accepted by Bob.

A stream is deleted by setting its port to zero. When Bob deletes the video stream from an audio and video session, the media line stays in the SDP with port 0 in both his second offer and Alice's second answer, leaving an audio-only session. The RFC also notes that if both streams of an offer had been accepted, Alice would have sent a second offer declining one of them.
sections.eli5: To add video, you add a new line to the note. To drop video, you keep the line but write zero as its port, which means no thanks.

sections.title: Third Party Call Control
sections.content:
Third Party Call Control (3pcc, RFC 3725) flows are common, and hold and resume flows are common in them. Three examples are given.

  • An offer with no media lines is answered with no media lines. In the second exchange Alice adds an audio stream that Bob accepts.
  • Alice's first offer has connection address 0.0.0.0 and a random port number, so Bob cannot send media to her (the stream is "black holed"). In the second exchange she changes the address and a media session is established.
  • The same idea in reverse: Bob's answer carries 0.0.0.0, so Alice cannot send media to him, until Bob changes the address in a second offer.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a helper sets up the call between two people. The helper can start with an address that means nowhere, then swap in the real address when everyone is ready.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Offers and answers can contain private information about addresses and sessions. If that must stay private, the protocol carrying them must provide security. For SIP, this means TLS transport and/or S/MIME encryption of the SDP body.

Offers and answers also need to be properly authenticated and authorized before they are used to set up a media session. The RFC names SIP Digest, certificates and cryptographically-verified SIP identity as examples of SIP mechanisms.
sections.eli5: The notes say who is calling from where, so they should be kept private, and you should check who sent them.

data.title: Alice's offer
data.code:
v=0
o=alice 2890844526 2890844526 IN IP4 host.atlanta.example.com
s=
c=IN IP4 host.atlanta.example.com
t=0 0
m=audio 49170 RTP/AVP 0 8 97
a=rtpmap:0 PCMU/8000
a=rtpmap:8 PCMA/8000
a=rtpmap:97 iLBC/8000
m=video 51372 RTP/AVP 31 32
a=rtpmap:31 H261/90000
a=rtpmap:32 MPV/90000

messages.label: Second answer
messages.note: Alice uses a new port; media is active.
